headline: 6/10 multisig controls 10-day timelock for T1 upgrades on UUPS proxies (weETH/eETH owner)

findings.text: Timelock at 0x9f26d4C958fD811A1F59B01B86Be7dFFc9d20761 is owner of weETH (0xCd5fE23C85820F7B72D0926FC9b05b43E359b7ee), eETH, RoleRegistry; minDelay=864000s (10 days) via getMinDelay() at block 25184477 (https://defipunkd.com/address/1/0x9f26d4C958fD811A1F59B01B86Be7dFFc9d20761). 6/10 Safe at 0xcdd57D11476c22d265722F68390b036f3DA48c21 holds PROPOSER_ROLE and EXECUTOR_ROLE on timelock (hasRole true at block 25184506).

Multiple UUPS proxies (e.g. RoleRegistry 0x62247D29B4B9BECf4BB73E0c722cf6445cfC7cE9, oracle executor 0x0EF8fa4760Db8f5Cd4d993f3e3416f30f942D705 implementation 0xd50f28485A75A1FdE432BA7d012d0E2543D2f20d); timelock itself immutable (no proxy). Upgrade path reaches fund-holding contracts.

Execution path: 6/10 multisig calls schedule (proposer) on timelock -> 10-day MIN_DELAY wait (getMinDelay=864000s) -> multisig calls execute (executor). Uncontested fast-path delay = 10 days. No additional timelock layers or on-chain governor found.

Primary control multisig: 6/10 Safe (threshold 6/10, version 1.3.0) at 0xcdd57D11476c22d265722F68390b036f3DA48c21 holds timelock proposer/executor roles; legacy 2/6 Safe at 0xF155a2632Ef263a6A382028B3B33feb29175b8A5 noted in prior reports. No other emergency multisigs enumerated on upgrade path.

No active on-chain Governor / token-weighted voting for protocol upgrades; ETHFI token exists (0xFe0c30065B384F05761f15d0CC899D4F9F9Cc0eB) but no proposal/voting constants or timelock governance path found in reads or docs.

No separate emergency-pause guardian with distinct time cap identified on main timelock or weETH; pause functions exist on peripheral contracts (e.g. oracle executor) but not confirmed on core upgrade surface.

Highest tier T1: upgradeTo/upgradeToAndCall on weETH/eETH (fund-holding UUPS proxies owned by timelock) reachable via multisig + 10d timelock path. Also controls RoleRegistry and node/membership managers.

steelman.red: 6/10 multisig (team-managed per docs) unilaterally controls T1 upgrade surface on all user-fund contracts with no on-chain governance check or broad signer distribution.
steelman.orange: 10-day timelock delay provides exit window before any upgrade executes; multisig threshold (60%) and size (10 signers) raise bar above 2-of-3 but fall short of full Security Council criteria (unknown non-insider %).
steelman.green: Long 10-day uncontested delay on T1 actions plus high-threshold multisig allows users to exit weETH before changes; timelock is transparent and on-chain verifiable.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because T1 upgrade authority exists on fund-holding contracts via 6/10 multisig + 10-day timelock (C3,C7); delay meets 7-day bar but controlling multisig does not qualify as Security Council (unknown signer composition) and no active on-chain governance token voting path exists (C5), per Hard Rule 13 and grade rules.

evidence.shows: EtherFiTimelock; getMinDelay()=864000s (10 days); roles and AccessControl at block 25184477; not proxy.

protocol_metadata.about: Liquid restaking protocol where users deposit ETH to receive weETH (value-accruing liquid restaked ETH) or eETH. Assets are staked on Ethereum and restaked via AVS operators for additional yield while remaining liquid and composable in DeFi. Non-custodial with permissionless redeem paths.

headline: Permissionless burn/redeem of weETH/eETH with validator exit queue; pause scope and claim gating unclear on main contracts

findings.text: Main exit functions: burn eETH/weETH to redeem ETH from LiquidityPool (0x308861A430be4cce5502d0A12724771Fc6DaF216); request full unstake queues validator exits; anyone can call distribute after beacon finalization (docs).
Redeem/burn is permissionless (no onlyRole or whitelist in core flows per docs and on-chain reads); new-request placement vs finalized-claim distinction exists (queue for insufficient unbonded ETH).

Pause functions confirmed on peripheral contracts (e.g. oracle executor 0x0EF8fa4760Db8f5Cd4d993f3e3416f30f942D705 has pause/unPause); no explicit PAUSE_ROLE holder or infinite-pause confirmation on weETH/LiquidityPool in reads.
No clear separation of fast emergency pause (capped) vs governance pause found; multisig controls many roles but no time-capped guardian explicitly tied to exit claims.
Queued redemptions documented: process from unbonded ETH or full validator exits; no daily cap stated but beacon-chain finalization delay inherent; queue itself not confirmed pausable.
No explicit forced-exit/escape-hatch beyond standard redeem + anyone-can-distribute finalized ETH; no adversarial-admin permissionless bypass found.
Exit functions directly callable on-chain (Etherscan write tab or wallet); no frontend dependency required per docs and permissionless design.

steelman.red: Multisig or roles could pause new redemptions or claims indefinitely with no on-chain time cap or governance override visible.
steelman.orange: Redeem/burn is permissionless and finalized claims distributable by anyone; any pause appears scoped to requests or peripherals, with 10-day timelock on broader changes providing exit window.
steelman.green: Fully permissionless on-chain exit path exists for weETH/eETH; users can always burn and claim finalized ETH without admin signature or frontend.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because core redeem/burn and finalized distribution are permissionless and on-chain (E1,E2,E7) with no evidence of indefinite claim pause, but pause scope/actor on main LiquidityPool/weETH and exact queue pausability remain undetermined after checklist (E3-E5), meeting orange criteria for broad-scope pausability uncertainty.

evidence.shows: Redeeming eETH/weETH: burn to withdraw from unbonded ETH or queue validator exits; anyone can distribute finalized ETH; permissionless process
Unstake flow for weETH/eETH: request, queue, claim after period; direct on-chain steps described
Liquidity pool address (core for redemptions); surfaced in multiple proxy reads
Peripheral contract with explicit pause/unPause functions and roles
Withdraw or transfer vaults with ease; non-custodial liquid staking

unknowns: E3: exact PAUSE_ROLE holder and whether infinite pause callable on weETH or LiquidityPool (only peripheral pause confirmed)
E4: emergency vs governance pause distinction and time caps on exit paths
E5: whether redemption queue itself is pausable by multisig or roles

headline: ~100% TVS exposed to 9 permissioned node operators + EigenLayer AVS slashing; oracle executor and beacon substrate mitigate but do not eliminate principal risk

findings.text: Core external calls: beacon chain Deposit/Withdrawal (substrate), EigenLayer AVS for restaking (via node operator manager 0xd5edf7730ABAd812247F6F54D7bd31a52554e35E), oracle executor 0x0EF8fa4760Db8f5Cd4d993f3e3416f30f942D705 for reports (latestReportRefBlock etc.). Failure of oracle or AVS mis-report can affect rebase/yield but not direct mint of unbacked.

9 professional permissioned node operators (from protocol docs); small curated set with no on-chain diversification proof or insurance in reads. Misbehavior/slashing can impair principal in restaked positions (A4 depth). Oracle executor committee/role-managed but single-contract surface.
No material non-canonical bridge dependency for core staking (L2 weETH via LayerZero in separate repo but not primary TVS path); main TVS on Ethereum.
Restaking depth: ETH -> eETH/weETH -> EigenLayer AVS operators (1-2 levels); slashing at operator/AVS level propagates to user principal in weETH (no per-market silo isolation for core restake).
No forkedFrom in DeFiLlama context; original liquid restaking design.

Fallbacks: unbonded ETH buffer in LiquidityPool for redemptions; postReportWaitTimeInSlots (50) on oracle executor; acceptableRebaseAprInBps=500 sanity. No live second-oracle or rebase bound enforcement confirmed active in reads; many are deployed but activation status unknown.
No appchain/sequencer; inherits Ethereum L1 liveness (substrate, not dependency).
No critical keeper/relayer liveness for core exit (permissionless distribute after beacon finalization); auto-compound in vaults is UX, not principal-critical.

Governance-mutable (multisig via timelock): can update node operator set, AVS registrations, oracle executor address (via RoleRegistry and manager contracts); 10-day timelock provides exit window before new dependency introduced.

steelman.red: 9 permissioned operators + EigenLayer AVS create direct slashing path to 100% TVS principal; small set and no on-chain insurance make external failure catastrophic.
steelman.orange: Diversified 9-operator set + unbonded buffer + 10-day timelock on operator/AVS changes bound principal loss and give exit window; oracle sanity checks (postReportWait) mitigate but not eliminate yield/price impact.
steelman.green: All critical paths have on-chain buffers, permissionless finalization, and long timelock on mutable dependencies; no single external actor can freeze or steal principal without diversified failure.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because external dependencies (A2: 9 permissioned NOs, A4: EigenLayer AVS slashing, A1: oracle executor) can cause principal loss or yield freeze on ~100% TVS, but diversification, LiquidityPool buffer, and 10-day timelock on changes (A9) prevent unmitigated catastrophic single-point failure, per grade anchors (Stage 1 equivalent, impacted TVS bounded/recoverable).

evidence.shows: 9 professional permissioned node operators; full withdrawals queue validator exits; oracle/report handling with postReportWaitTimeInSlots=50 and acceptableRebaseAprInBps=500

unknowns: A2: exact operator set size/diversification metrics and slashing insurance/bonding on-chain (docs state 9 but no live verification)
A6: activation status of rebase/oracle circuit breakers (params exist but not confirmed enforcing today)
A9: whether node operator/AVS registry changes are timelock-protected or direct multisig (inferred via RoleRegistry)

headline: Fully permissionless contracts (no whitelist/KYC on deposit/redeem); independent paths via DEX/wallets/aggregators exist despite frontend ToS

findings.text: No onlyWhitelisted, onlyRole, or KYC modifiers on core user entry/exit (deposit to weETH/eETH, burn/redeem) per docs and on-chain reads; all flows permissionless.
No off-chain operator approval required for admission (deposit/redeem/claim); oracle/node reports affect settlement but not admission gate. Permissionless distribute after beacon finalization.

Frontend ToS (gitbook) contains standard sanctions/jurisdiction boilerplate (A3-passive); no evidence of active IP geo-blocking or wallet screening on official UI in fetches. Reported as context only.

Independent paths confirmed: weETH tradable on DEXes (Uniswap etc.), wallet integrations (MetaMask), aggregators (DeFiLlama, 1inch), third-party frontends; direct Etherscan write for burn/redeem; no published SDK but contract-level access sufficient.
No on-chain blocklist or OFAC check in contracts (no sanctions oracle integration found).
Read access fully permissionless (anyone can view balances, reports); write access (deposit/redeem) also permissionless.

ToS URL: https://etherfi.gitbook.io/etherfi/ether.fi-legal/terms-of-use; verbatim eligibility clause not extractable due to SPA render but standard 'comply with applicable law / restricted jurisdictions' language present per risk disclosures page.

steelman.red: Official frontend ToS and any potential wallet screening could block users; no on-chain KYC but practical access gated by publisher policies.
steelman.orange: Contracts permissionless but no published SDK or third-party frontend dominance makes it operationally captured by official UI.
steelman.green: Core contracts admit any address unconditionally for deposit/redeem/distribute; multiple independent on-chain paths (DEX, wallets, Etherscan) exist without publisher cooperation.

rationale.verdict: Choosing green because no contract-level whitelist/KYC or operator gate on any user action (A1,A2,A5), and independent access paths (DEX/wallets/aggregators) are live and permissionless (A3b), satisfying default green rule regardless of frontend ToS (A3 context only).

Direct on-chain unstake/claim steps; no KYC or approval required
Non-custodial; stake/redeem flows open; composable in 400+ DeFi protocols
Standard ToS with jurisdictional/sanctions eligibility language (A3-passive)
weETH ERC-20 (permissionless transfer/burn)

unknowns: A3: exact runtime enforcement (IP blocking or Chainalysis screening) on official frontend (not visible in static fetches)
A6: verbatim full ToS sanctions clause (SPA render limited extraction)

findings.text: All pinned addresses verified: Timelock (Etherscan), RoleRegistry (Sourcify), weETH/eETH proxies (Etherscan ABI), oracle executor (Etherscan); proxy + implementation pairs resolved in /api/contract/abi responses.

GitHub repo https://github.com/etherfi-protocol/smart-contracts matches structure (Solidity, UUPS, AccessControl, Timelock patterns) but no exact commit SHA pinned or bytecode diff performed in this run.
No audit_links in per-protocol context; website claims 'audited by industry-leading firms' but no specific firm, date, or report URL fetched or verifiable in this run.
No recognized-firm audit (Trail of Bits, Zellic, etc.) confirmed; unknown-firm or self-audit possible but not evidenced.
Post-audit drift cannot be assessed (no baseline audit commit or recent diff sampled); recent GitHub activity (May 2026) but no material-change analysis possible.
Proxies verified with implementation surfaced (e.g. oracle executor impl 0xd50f28485A75A1FdE432BA7d012d0E2543D2f20d); timelock immutable (direct contract).

steelman.red: No audit report or commit correspondence verifiable; reliance on 'industry-leading' claim without evidence.
steelman.orange: All core bytecode verified on explorers and open-source repo exists with matching architecture; missing current audit and exact commit pin prevent green.
steelman.green: Full verification on Etherscan/Sourcify for every pinned address + public GitHub repo allows independent inspection of deployed logic.

rationale.verdict: Choosing orange because bytecode is verified on explorers for proxies and implementation (V1,V6), open-source repo matches (V2), but no specific audit from recognized firm covering current deployment is evidenced (V3-V4) and no commit SHA or drift check possible (V5), per grade rules.
